channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] Sandworm and Qilin are inside Cisco firewall management: a critical auth bypass, exploited since August
item.category: Top Story
item.description: Cisco and CISA confirmed on Wednesday that CVE-2026-20079 — a critical authentication bypass in Secure Firewall Management Center, patched back in March — has been exploited since August. Crafted HTTP requests reach a process created at boot and hand an unauthenticated attacker root on the appliance that configures your firewalls. Cisco Talos attributes three activity clusters: one deploying a web shell to harvest credentials, one tied to the Russian state group Sandworm delivering Cyclops Blink, and one linked to Qilin ransomware staging encryption target lists. CISA added the flaw to KEV with a 12 September federal deadline. For OT defenders the significance is not the firewall — it is the management plane above it. Whoever holds FMC holds the rule set separating enterprise from plant, and can rewrite it without touching a single controller. - CVE-2026-20079 - Patched Mar 2026; exploitation began Aug 2026; Cisco and Talos disclosure and KEV addition 9 Sep 2026; reported 10 Sep 2026, 6:06 AM ET — verified 11 Sep 2026, 7:00 AM ET

item.title: [High] Boston Scientific puts a number on it: production is mostly back, and the quarter is not — guidance withdrawn two weeks after an IT-side intrusion
item.category: Incident — IT-side compromise, manufacturing disruption; medical device sector
item.description: The recovery curve and the cost curve have now separated. In an 8 September securities filing the company said it is unlikely to meet the third-quarter and full-year sales-growth and adjusted-EPS ranges it issued in July, expects to recapture only some of the lost revenue as it works down backlog, and still has no date for full recovery; a revised outlook is deferred to the 28 October earnings call. Operationally the picture is better than a week ago: its own weekend update reports distribution substantially restored, major centres shipping at or above normal levels, manufacturing restored across most global facilities and all sterilisation sites running. Access is still assessed as confined to internal-facing IT, with no controller or implanted-device function affected, and no entry route, vulnerability or extortion claim named. Nothing touched a control system, and roughly a fortnight of output is gone anyway. - Boston Scientific incident page and 8 Sep 2026 SEC filing, reported by MedTech Dive - Detected 25 Aug 2026; disclosed 26 Aug 2026; manufacturing disruption confirmed 28 Aug 2026; shipping restoration reported 4 Sep 2026; guidance withdrawn in SEC filing 8 Sep 2026 — re-verified 11 Sep 2026, 7:00 AM ET

item.title: [Critical] The water campaign, quantified: CISA counts 100-plus internet-exposed systems hit, with controller logic and alarms altered
item.category: Incident — Confirmed OT disruption, water sector; CISA-quantified scale
item.description: CISA has put a figure on July’s campaign against US water utilities: malicious activity against more than 100 internet-exposed systems in the Water and Wastewater Systems sector, commonly programmable logic controllers wired straight into a cellular modem. The FBI records incidents at utilities in at least seven states since 27 July, with reporting placing targeting across at least a dozen. Some degraded operations — lost pressure, flooding, plants run by hand — though supply was not widely interrupted, and in several intrusions actors altered controllers to disable shutdown processes and alarms, letting unsafe conditions develop unannounced. US officials assess Iranian actors as likely responsible and describe the activity as largely opportunistic. It stays on the page five weeks on because of the admission behind the number: the exposure that carried it was in nobody’s asset register. - CISA exposure-reduction guidance and the FBI/EPA public service announcement — corroborated by SecurityWeek, Cybersecurity Dive, TechCrunch and The Register; Minnesota impact detail from state officials and SecurityWeek - Scale confirmed and reported 26 Aug 2026; observed activity July 2026; FBI PSA issued 30 Jul 2026 — re-verified 11 Sep 2026, 7:00 AM ET

item.title: [High] The water campaign was not the whole campaign — telecoms and energy control systems are now being probed, and there is a $10 million bounty on the man said to run it
item.category: Targeting — Iran-linked campaign widens beyond water into telecommunications and energy; attempts reported, no confirmed OT impact
item.description: Two developments this week moved the summer’s dominant OT story past the water sector. NBC News reported on 2 September, citing four people with access to government and industry threat information, that Iran-linked operators have spent recent weeks probing internet-facing automated control systems at telecommunications and energy providers as well as water utilities — and that those attempts have so far been unsuccessful. A day later the State Department’s Rewards for Justice programme posted a reward of up to $10 million for information identifying or locating Amir Yaryab, named as head of the cyber operations division of the IRGC Cyber-Electronic Command and accused of directing groups including the CyberAv3ngers persona against US critical infrastructure. Separately, a Telegram channel presenting itself as a voice for Iranian cyber operations has threatened action against US energy, water and telecommunications, without evidence of any successful operation. The signal for defenders is the change of aim, not a new capability: the same tradecraft that found exposed water PLCs in July is now being pointed at neighbouring sectors that run the same internet-facing gear. - NBC News reporting on expanded targeting and the State Department Rewards for Justice announcement, as carried by The Record — water-campaign scale from CISA and SecurityWeek - NBC report 2 Sep 2026; $10 million reward announced 3 Sep 2026 — verified 11 Sep 2026, 7:00 AM ET

item.title: [Critical] A small UK generating station ran manually for four days after an Iran-linked cyberattack
item.category: Incident — Confirmed OT disruption, power generation (UK)
item.description: A small British power generating station was taken offline for four days by a cyberattack, with staff forced to restore operations manually. The Telegraph broke the story on 22 August; the UK government confirmed that a small-scale generator had been affected while stating there was at no point a risk to the national energy system, and the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero has since contacted power companies about the risk. UK assessments reported by the Telegraph point to hackers affiliated with the Iranian regime, likely the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The site’s size is the uncomfortable part rather than a reassurance: distributed generation, embedded generators and behind-the-meter assets sit below most reporting thresholds, are often remotely operated by a third party, and are numerous enough that an attack that works once is repeatable. - SecurityWeek and CNBC, both citing the originating Telegraph report and the UK government statement - Incident occurred July 2026; reported 22–23 Aug 2026; government response reported 24 Aug 2026 — re-verified 11 Sep 2026, 7:00 AM ET

item.title: [Medium] A Bavarian municipal utility was encrypted a week ago and kept the lights and water on — the separation held, the office did not
item.category: Incident — Encryption event at a municipal multi-utility (Germany); IT only, electricity and water unaffected
item.description: Stadtwerke Landsberg, the city-owned utility for Landsberg am Lech, told customers on Monday that attackers encrypted its central IT network in an incident that began overnight on 1 September. The operator says electricity, water and its other essential services were never affected; office systems were, and staff remain reachable only intermittently by phone and email while external specialists complete a forensic investigation. No ransomware brand has been named and the utility has not said whether an extortion demand followed. It cannot yet rule out that customer data — names, addresses, contact details and bank details — was accessed. A comparable attack on the utility serving Kamen, Bönen and Bergkamen in North Rhine-Westphalia disrupted internal systems for weeks in late June. For OT defenders the useful detail is the one that did not make the headline: a small municipal multi-utility lost its business systems and still ran supply, which is the outcome segmentation is supposed to produce and the one worth confirming you could reproduce. - The Record from Recorded Future News, citing the Stadtwerke Landsberg customer notice - Incident began 1 Sep 2026; disclosed by the utility and reported 8 Sep 2026 — verified 11 Sep 2026, 7:00 AM ET

item.title: [Critical] Five agencies say the S7 family is being actively hunted — and that the exploit scripts are being written with AI
item.category: NSA/CISA/FBI/DOE/EPA joint advisory AA26-231A — active targeting of Siemens S7 series PLCs
item.description: The joint advisory published on 19 August is the primary-source anchor under this edition’s AI research. The NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE and EPA report threat actors actively working against Siemens S7 controllers that are internet-exposed or poorly segmented, spanning the S7‑200, ‑300, ‑400, ‑1200 and ‑1500 lines, and name Critical Manufacturing, Energy, Water and Wastewater, Chemical, Food and Agriculture and Commercial Facilities as the most affected sectors. What makes it notable is the method: the agencies describe AI‑generated reconnaissance and exploitation scripts built around the open-source python‑snap7 library and disguised to look like legitimate OT monitoring tooling. Two familiar conditions do the enabling — internet exposure through weak segmentation, and default or weak credentials. The protocol expertise that used to gate ICS exploit development is no longer the barrier. - CISA joint advisory AA26-231A (NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE, EPA) — corroborated by SecurityWeek, Tenable and Infosecurity Magazine - Published 19 Aug 2026 — re-verified 11 Sep 2026, 7:00 AM ET

item.title: [High] A frontier model ported a working PLC exploit to a second controller in eight hours — then bricked it
item.category: Forescout Vedere Labs — AI-assisted exploit development against PLCs
item.description: Forescout’s Vedere Labs published the result of a deliberately awkward experiment: point a frontier AI model at real industrial hardware and see how far it gets. Starting from the team’s own remote code execution exploit for a WAGO 750-852, built on CVE-2021-31886 — a pre-authentication overflow in the Nucleus FTP server — they asked Claude to port it to the related 750-831, giving the model a terminal, Ghidra and the physical device. It worked, but not cleanly. The first model tried failed to trace the vulnerable function; a stronger model eventually worked out why the injected shellcode was being wiped before it could run, and once past that it produced two working payloads in twelve minutes. Total cost of the final stage: over eight hours and more than $500 in API charges. A follow-up attempt at a command-and-control implant wrote to flash and permanently bricked the PLC. - Forescout Research – Vedere Labs report, via SecurityWeek — corroborated by Cybersecurity Dive with direct comment from Vedere Labs - Published 1 Sep 2026; corroborating reporting 1–2 Sep 2026 — verified 11 Sep 2026, 7:00 AM ET

item.title: [High] The quartermaster model: US authorities seize the platforms a China-nexus group used to scan power companies, telecoms and a water district
item.category: DOJ/FBI takedown and NSA/FBI advisory — QTFY, a China-nexus scanning and proxy operation against US critical infrastructure
item.description: The FBI and Justice Department have seized domains behind QTFY, a state-backed Chinese operation that ran two platforms — QScan for reconnaissance and QTRouter for traffic relay — across a campaign lasting years. Court records name telecommunications firms, hospitals, defence contractors, power companies and financial institutions among the critical-infrastructure targets, alongside federal agencies including the Department of Energy. QScan infected thousands of internet-of-things devices worldwide and enrolled them into the QTRouter relay network, alongside leased proxies and virtual private servers, which is what kept the operation’s origin hidden for years. The NSA and FBI say the operators used zero-day and n-day flaws for initial access, then stole legitimate credentials for persistence — a Check Point Quantum Gateway flaw to scan power and telecommunications firms, Ivanti Cloud Services Appliance zero-days against DOE and health research labs, and a BeyondTrust flaw against a US state government, with a water district also targeted. Researchers at Black Lotus Labs, which tracked the group for years and supported the takedown, describe a “quartermaster model”: reconnaissance, proxy orchestration and operational routing run as one service, sold on to the People’s Liberation Army and the Ministry of State Security. The relevance for OT is the shape rather than the victim list — the edge and IoT estate that most operators do not inventory was both the target set and the infrastructure. - CVE-2024-24919 - Seizure and advisory announced 26–27 Aug 2026; reported 27 Aug 2026 — verified 11 Sep 2026, 7:00 AM ET

item.title: [Info] The federal answer to the distribution edge arrives as a research agreement, not a rule — automated data engineering and machine detection for grid operators
item.category: DOE CESER and Sandia National Laboratories — Communications and Cybersecurity for the Energy Edge (C2E2)
item.description: The Department of Energy’s Office of Cybersecurity, Energy Security, and Emergency Response and Sandia National Laboratories announced an agreement on 8 September covering Communications and Cybersecurity for the Energy Edge, or C2E2 — work aimed at automating the grid data engineering that utility operators currently do by hand, and at applying machine learning to threat detection across distribution and edge assets. The reported figure attached to the detection work is 95 per cent accuracy. Treat that number as a laboratory result rather than a field one: the announcement does not publish the dataset, the false-positive rate, or the operating conditions behind it, and grid detection benchmarks rarely survive contact with a real distribution feeder unchanged. The reason it still matters to a working defender is the problem it names. The distribution edge — reclosers, capacitor bank controllers, DER inverters, feeder RTUs — is where asset inventory is weakest and where the July water-sector campaign showed what exposed, unmonitored controllers cost. Federal research money moving toward automated visibility at that layer is a signal about where the next round of guidance and, eventually, funding will land. - DOE CESER and Sandia National Laboratories announcement, reported by Industrial Cyber - Announced and reported 8 Sep 2026 — verified 11 Sep 2026, 7:00 AM ET

item.title: [Critical] September’s ICS Patch Tuesday reaches the safety controller: a CVSS 9.2 authentication flaw in Schneider’s Modicon M580
item.category: Schneider Modicon M580 / M580 Safety — CVE-2026-3869, CVSS 9.2, not exploited
item.description: Schneider Electric, Siemens and Aveva published their September advisories on 8 September, and the one that matters most sits inside a controller family run on safety duty. CVE-2026-3869, rated CVSS 9.2, is an authentication weakness in the Modicon M580 and M580 Safety ranges — the mid-tier PLC that runs a great many water, power and process plants, and the same hardware many sites rely on for safety functions. Schneider also fixed high-severity defects in PowerLogic T300 and EcoStruxure IT Data Center Expert, and finally shipped Modicon MC80 patches for weaknesses first disclosed as far back as 2019. Siemens added four critical advisories, including the Reyrolle 7SR5 protection relay. Nothing here is exploited. What makes it consequential is where it lands: on the devices whose failure mode is physical, not informational — and on a patch clock measured in validated outages rather than days. - CVE-2026-3869 - Vendor advisories published 8 Sep 2026; roundup published 9 Sep 2026, 6:49 AM ET — verified 11 Sep 2026, 7:00 AM ET

item.title: [Critical] The other remote-access box just went live: public exploit code for a NetScaler auth bypass, and attacks the same week
item.category: Citrix NetScaler ADC/Gateway — CVE-2026-19490, CVSS 9.3, exploitation confirmed
item.description: Citrix patched CVE-2026-19490 on 19 August — an authentication bypass, CVSS 9.3, in NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances configured as a Gateway (SSL VPN, ICA Proxy, CVPN or RDP Proxy) or as an AAA virtual server, with SAML configurations among those affected. For a fortnight it stayed theoretical. Then public exploit code appeared in early September, and on 3 September sensor operators began recording bypass attempts from multiple source addresses across four countries, with reporting on 4 September confirming attackers had turned to the flaw in the wild. NetScaler is not an OT product, but it is very often the thing an engineer authenticates through before reaching a jump host, a historian or a vendor session — which makes an unauthenticated bypass on it a route to the plant, not merely to the corporate estate. - Citrix security bulletin, corroborated by BleepingComputer, SecurityWeek and Help Net Security; exploitation telemetry reported by sensor operators - Patched 19 Aug 2026; exploit code public early Sep 2026; exploitation observed 3 Sep 2026; active targeting reported 4 Sep 2026; added to CISA KEV 9 Sep 2026 — verified 11 Sep 2026, 7:00 AM ET

item.title: [Critical] CERT Polska confirms attackers are taking full control of internet-facing MikroTik routers — the box that quietly backhauls half the remote sites in your fleet
item.category: MikroTik RouterOS — “MikroTrick” pre-auth SSH takeover chain, confirmed exploited since 2 Sep
item.description: CERT Polska disclosed six RouterOS vulnerabilities on 5 September and confirmed that two of them are already being chained in live attacks. The chain, named MikroTrick, pairs CVE-2026-67276 (CVSS 9.2) — RouterOS validated only part of an SSH RSA public key, so an attacker who knows a username and the key’s public modulus can forge a key and log in without the private half — with CVE-2026-86060 (CVSS 9.2), a username-parsing flaw that hands the resulting session full administrative rights. Together they give unauthenticated device takeover wherever SSH answers from the internet. A third flaw, CVE-2026-67277 (CVSS 8.8), leaks kernel memory or reboots the device through the unauthenticated bandwidth-test service. MikroTik patched on 3 September in 6.49.21, 7.23.4, 7.24.2 and 7.25beta3. CERT Polska says confirmed compromises trace to 82.192.72.4 and run back to at least 2 September. This matters in OT because RouterOS is the cheap, ubiquitous router behind remote pump stations, substations, wellheads, irrigation skids and contractor-built field cabinets — equipment that is frequently outside the OT asset register and reachable from the internet by design. - CERT Polska (CSIRT NASK) warning and its companion CVE page, with MikroTik’s September 2026 security bulletin — corroborated by The Hacker News and Security Affairs - Patches released 3 Sep 2026; CERT Polska exploitation warning published 5 Sep 2026; attacks observed since at least 2 Sep 2026 — verified 11 Sep 2026, 7:00 AM ET

item.title: [Critical] CISA put SonicWall’s exploited SMA1000 pair in KEV a day after disclosure — a CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw chained to code execution
item.category: SonicWall SMA1000 — Two zero-days exploited, CVSS 10 chain, now in CISA KEV
item.description: SonicWall disclosed on 1 September that two previously unknown vulnerabilities in its SMA1000 secure remote access gateway and SSL-VPN appliance have been exploited in the wild, and CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 2 September as part of a seven-CVE batch. CVE-2026-83548, carrying a CVSS score of 10, is a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Appliance Work Place interface that lets an unauthenticated attacker reach sensitive functionality; CVE-2026-83549, at 7.8, is an OS command injection flaw in the Appliance Management Console that an authenticated attacker can turn into remote code execution. SonicWall says it observed exploitation of both, which points to the pair being chained for unauthenticated code execution on the appliance. The vendor found the flaws and the attacks internally, and has published no indicators of compromise. Models 6210, 7210 and 8200v are affected. For OT operators this is the exact class of device that vendor engineers, integrators and on-call staff use to reach the plant from outside — a box that sits at the boundary, terminates trusted sessions and is rarely covered by an OT change window. - SonicWall PSIRT advisory SNWLID-2026-0016 and the CISA KEV addition of 2 Sep 2026 — reported by SecurityWeek and Help Net Security - Advisory published 1 Sep 2026; added to CISA KEV 2 Sep 2026 — verified 11 Sep 2026, 7:00 AM ET

item.title: [Critical] A fourth boundary box in a fortnight: a CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw in the platform your outsourced IT uses to reach every machine you own
item.category: N-able N-central — CVE-2026-86218 (CVSS 10.0) unauthenticated remote code execution; exploitation reported
item.description: N-able disclosed CVE-2026-86218 on 6 September and rated it CVSS 10.0 — an unauthenticated attacker can execute code on an internet-exposed N-central server, in a low-complexity attack requiring no credentials and no user interaction. The fix is N-central 2026.3 Hotfix 4, build 2026.3.1.14, and reporting notes it is the fourth N-central hotfix in roughly five weeks. Huntress reported a compromised production environment but could not establish which of the disclosed flaws was used, and flagged this one as a possible zero-day alongside two high-severity issues; N-able’s own notice describes exploitation observed in the wild. The Shadowserver Foundation tracks close to 1,500 internet-exposed N-central servers, most in the United States and Europe. N-central is a remote monitoring and management platform — an agent with system-level rights on every endpoint it manages. For industrial sites, the question is whether the managed service provider that patches your engineering workstations, historians and plant IT runs one, and whether their console is reachable from the internet. - N-able security advisory and incident notice, reported by BleepingComputer and SecurityWeek — KEV listing from CISA’s 8 Sep 2026 catalogue update; exposure count from the Shadowserver Foundation - Disclosed and hotfix released 6 Sep 2026; exploitation reported the same day; added to CISA KEV 8 Sep 2026 — verified 11 Sep 2026, 7:00 AM ET

item.title: [High] CISA’s 3 September batch lands on the remote-access client itself — a CVSS 9.6 root-level flaw in IXON VPN
item.category: CISA ICS advisory batch — ICSA-26-246 series; industrial remote access, SCADA platform, engineering tooling
item.description: The five advisories CISA published on 3 September are worth reading in a particular order, because the first one sits on the exact attack path two national agencies spent last week warning about. ICSA-26-246-02 covers CVE-2026-75925 in the IXON VPN Client below 1.4.7, rated CVSS v3.1 9.6: the client’s local configuration interface accepts changes without authenticating the requester, and does not neutralise line-ending sequences before writing them to a file that a privileged subprocess later consumes — so an attacker can inject extra directives and have commands run as root or SYSTEM. The injected configuration survives reboots, and the VPN keeps working normally, so nothing about the machine’s behaviour tells the engineer using it that anything changed. This is the software sitting on maintenance laptops and engineering workstations that reach machines in the field. The rest of the batch is more routine but not trivial: ICSA-26-246-06 flags CVE-2026-77393 in Inductive Automation Ignition 8.1.53 and earlier at CVSS 8.8, where the Gateway’s Create Project Role(s) setting shipped blank and any authenticated user able to run gateway scripts can create projects; ICSA-26-246-03 covers CVE-2026-12663 in Rockwell ControlFLASH 15.07 and earlier, whose installer granted the Everyone group write access to a product directory; ICSA-26-246-01 covers CVE-2026-77477 in the OPC Foundation UA LocalDiscoveryServer installers; and ICSA-26-246-08 covers a missing-authorization issue, CVE-2026-82684, in Tycon Systems TPDIN-Monitor-WEB3 2.2.9 and earlier that could expose credentials, configuration or flash contents. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-246-01, -02, -03, -06 and -08 — summarised by the Viakoo/Security Boulevard daily OT briefing; IXON technical detail cross-checked against the vendor security advisory page and CVE records - Advisories published 3 Sep 2026 — verified 11 Sep 2026, 7:00 AM ET

item.title: [High] CISA’s 1 September batch is five-sixths Rockwell — and it reaches the Logix controllers themselves
item.category: ICSA-26-244-01 to -05 + Rockwell PSIRT — a dozen-plus fixes, controllers included
item.description: CISA published eight ICS advisories on 1 September, and five of them are Rockwell Automation. The set covers RSLinx Classic (ICSA-26-244-01), the Redundancy Module Configuration Tool (-02), the Logix platform (-03), FactoryTalk Activation Manager (-04) and the ControlLogix, CompactLogix, CompactLogix 5480, GuardLogix and Compact GuardLogix controller families (-05). The RSLinx item is the one most sites will feel first: four flaws — CVE-2026-9621, CVE-2026-9622, CVE-2026-9624 and CVE-2026-9625 — let crafted Common Industrial Protocol traffic crash the communications service on version 4.50 and earlier, and it stays down until somebody restarts it by hand. RSLinx is the data path between controllers and the HMI, historian and engineering workstations, so a crash there is a visibility outage on a running process, not an IT inconvenience. The batch also carries an update to the Rockwell 1734 POINT I/O advisory (ICSA-26-202-09, Update A) and Update G to the long-running Mitsubishi Electric FA engineering software advisory (ICSA-24-135-04). Rockwell’s own round-up, reported 2 September, puts the total above a dozen fixes and adds detail the CISA summaries do not: remote code execution in FactoryTalk Historian, privilege escalation in FactoryTalk Activation Manager and in the Redundancy Module Configuration Tool, arbitrary code execution through the ControlFLASH firmware utility, cross-site scripting plus a web-server denial of service in ArmorStart distributed motor controllers, and further denial-of-service issues in 1756-ENBT and in Logix controllers via a third-party component. One item needs care rather than alarm: Rockwell’s advisory for CVE-2026-9637, a high-severity denial of service in ControlLogix and CompactLogix, is flagged as exploited in its document header but listed as not exploited in the body, and CISA states it is not aware of exploitation — read it as a documentation inconsistency, not a live campaign, and patch it on its merits. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-244-01 through -05 published 1 Sep 2026, plus ICSA-26-202-09 Update A and ICSA-24-135-04 Update G, read against the Rockwell Automation security advisory index and SecurityWeek’s 2 Sep 2026 round-up of the full Rockwell set - Published 1 Sep 2026 — verified 11 Sep 2026, 7:00 AM ET

item.title: [High] Microsoft ships its largest patch day on record, and the two flaws already being used are both local privilege escalation
item.category: Microsoft Patch Tuesday — two exploited Windows zero-days; HMI, engineering workstation and historian hosts
item.description: Microsoft’s September release closes roughly 973 vulnerabilities — the largest single Patch Tuesday it has published — with about 113 rated critical. Two are confirmed exploited in the wild, and both matter more to OT than their scores suggest. CVE-2026-81963 is an improper link-resolution flaw in the Windows Update Stack that lets a local attacker escalate to SYSTEM; it is reported as the first Windows Update Stack defect exploited as a zero-day. CVE-2026-85880 is a privilege-escalation flaw in Windows Advanced Local Procedure Call, rated CVSS 7.8, also giving SYSTEM. CISA added both to the KEV catalogue on 8 September with a 22 September federal remediation deadline. Neither is remotely exploitable on its own, which is precisely why they pair badly with the boundary devices elsewhere on this page: the exploited edge appliances supply the initial foothold, and these supply the jump to SYSTEM on the Windows host that host sits next to. In a plant that host is usually an HMI, an engineering workstation or a historian — machines that are rarely on a monthly patch cadence and often cannot be rebooted on demand. Two further items drew attention but are not confirmed exploited: CVE-2026-69829, a Windows Shell remote-code-execution flaw rated CVSS 9.8, and CVE-2026-69730 in Windows DNS, assessed as likely exploitable. - CVE-2026-81963 - Published 9 Sep 2026 — KEV additions 8 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] 117 reporting rules across 27 agencies — the number that explains why your incident-response plan has a lawyer on the critical path
item.description: A joint report published on 8 September by the McCrary Institute and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce puts a figure on something OT incident commanders have felt for years: citing a Government Accountability Office count, federal cyber incident reporting has grown to 117 regulations spread across 27 agencies, 48 of which apply to private industry. The argument is not that the requirements are illegitimate — the authors are explicit that Congress has already granted the necessary authorities — but that an organisation running an active response now operates two parallel systems at once: containment, which needs speed, and compliance, which needs the same facts restated across multiple federal channels on different clocks, definitions and thresholds. The recommendations centre on a single federal intake process led by CISA, use of CIRCIA’s existing “substantially similar” authority so one submission can satisfy comparable obligations, standardised definitions and timelines, and a strengthened role for the Cyber Incident Reporting Council, with the Office of the National Cyber Director driving alignment. The report is candid about the ceiling: statutory obligations, state law and international regimes cannot be harmonised away by executive action. For asset owners the timing matters because CISA is still finalising the CIRCIA rule, and this is a live input to that process rather than a retrospective critique. - McCrary Institute and U.S. Chamber of Commerce joint report, reported by Industrial Cyber — underlying counts attributed by the authors to a Government Accountability Office report - Published and reported 8 Sep 2026 — verified 11 Sep 2026, 7:00 AM ET

item.title: [Medium] The free assessment most small operators actually used has been withdrawn — the tool survives, the adviser who ran it does not
item.category: CISA — six free critical-infrastructure assessment services retired
item.description: CISA has confirmed that its regional staff will stop delivering six no-cost assessments offered to critical-infrastructure operators: Cyber Resilience Reviews, Cyber Resilience Essentials surveys, Ransomware Readiness Assessments, Incident Management Reviews, External Dependencies Management Assessments and Cyber Infrastructure Surveys. All six were run on site by a regional adviser using the Cyber Security Evaluation Tool (CSET) to produce a prioritised improvement report. In its statement the agency described the change as retiring legacy questionnaire assessments to reduce duplication, and said operators will be pointed instead to the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals. CSET itself remains open source, though the current release disables the retired assessment modules; older versions still run them, without an adviser to interpret the output. Field staff were told to stop at a 25 August internal meeting. The reporting notes the change lands amid a roughly one-third reduction in CISA’s workforce over the past year. - Cybersecurity Dive (original reporting, with CISA statement), corroborated by Utility Dive and Industrial Cyber - Published 1 Sep 2026, updated 3 Sep 2026 — re-verified 11 Sep 2026, 7:00 AM ET

item.title: [Info] The quantum migration arrives as a procurement problem — and OT owns the longest-lived keys in the building
item.description: On 3 September CISA and the G7 Cyber Expert Group published Preparing for the Post-Quantum Era: A Call to Action, urging governments and organisations to begin a phased, risk-based migration to post-quantum cryptography now rather than waiting for a cryptographically relevant quantum computer to exist. The reasoning that should land with defenders is harvest-now-decrypt-later: traffic captured today can be stored and decrypted once the capability arrives, so data with a long confidentiality life is already exposed. The first deliverable is unglamorous and familiar — a cryptographic inventory mapped to data lifetime, business criticality, protocol dependencies and vendor support. That is harder in OT than in IT for a structural reason: the assets are the long-lived ones. Controllers, RTUs, protective relays and gateways specified for fifteen to twenty-five years of service carry certificates, firmware-signing keys and VPN configurations that will outlast the entire migration window, and in many cases cannot be re-keyed without a vendor firmware release that does not yet exist. Europe’s roadmap expects member states to have taken first steps by 31 December 2026 and high-risk cases migrated no later than the end of 2030. - G7 Cyber Expert Group paper released with CISA — corroborated by Industrial Cyber, Infosecurity Magazine and ExecutiveGov - Published 3 Sep 2026 — verified 11 Sep 2026, 7:00 AM ET

item.title: [Medium] On Friday, anyone selling a connected product into the EU owes a 24-hour warning on exploited vulnerabilities
item.category: EU Cyber Resilience Act — Reporting obligations effective 11 Sep 2026
item.description: The EU Cyber Resilience Act enters its reporting phase this Friday, 11 September 2026 — four days from this edition. From that date, manufacturers of products with digital elements must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe security incidents affecting their products, with an early warning inside 24 hours and a fuller notification inside 72 hours. The scope reaches far past consumer IoT: PLCs, RTUs, drives, gateways, HMIs, protocol converters and the engineering software around them are products with digital elements, and the obligation follows the manufacturer regardless of where the affected device is installed. Legal analysts advise naming an owner now and building the assessment, escalation and customer-communication path in advance, coordinating it with existing NIS2 and GDPR duties rather than standing up a third parallel process. - Freshfields analysis via Lexology, surfaced in the Viakoo/Security Boulevard daily OT briefing - Analysis published 1 Sep 2026; obligations effective 11 Sep 2026 (forward-looking) — verified 11 Sep 2026, 7:00 AM ET

item.title: [Info] DOE opens the comment window on foreign-supplied grid equipment — and asks operators to define “remote access” for it
item.category: US Department of Energy, CESER — request for information on bulk-power-system supply-chain risk
item.description: The Department of Energy’s Office of Cybersecurity, Energy Security, and Emergency Response published a request for information in today’s Federal Register to inform how it implements the bulk-power-system executive order covering foreign-supplied equipment, which the notice cites as Executive Order 14421. The questions are the ones that decide whether the eventual rule is workable: what transactions should fall inside scope, how supply-chain risk should be assessed, and how to treat software and firmware, digital and maintenance services, and remote access. That last item is where asset owners have the most to contribute and the most to lose by staying quiet — vendor remote access into a substation is not one thing, and a definition written without operators in the room tends to capture routine relay-setting support and firmware delivery alongside the cases the order is actually aimed at. This is an RFI, not a rule or a directive: nothing is prohibited, no filing is required and no equipment becomes non-compliant today. Comments are due 9 October 2026, which gives utilities, co-ops, integrators and OEMs a month to respond. - US Department of Energy, Office of Cybersecurity, Energy Security, and Emergency Response — Federal Register notice, surfaced in the Viakoo/Security Boulevard daily OT briefing - Published 9 Sep 2026; comments due 9 Oct 2026 — verified 11 Sep 2026, 7:00 AM ET
